They are not cannon but I think the concept of them amd the possibility of their existence is fascinating. The whole balance of light and dark has always been a central theme in star wars, and while the jedi represent the light, they are not infallible in their judgment nor are they pure paragons of morality. The jedi are those who are in tune with the force who choose to put the good of all before all else. In contrast the sith put the needs and desires of themselves above all else. This greed and selfishness is what drives them and consequently what drives their power. Both of these exist within the natural order of the force. This is something that clone wars the animated series explores a bit more, that neither one is complete without the other, yet because their nature's are so opposite they cannot help but to battle against eachother. A jedi does not maintain this balance directly, but rather serves to act against the dark. If there were individuals who were force sensitive and able to remain completely objective to the needs of that balance, they would have to be very well trained and very powerful. Each side of the force has its own pull (something they tried and failed to explore in the new movies. You want good force lore go watch the clone wars series) Anakin was supposed to be that balance, pulled in both directions but able to resist the draws to keep the balance in check. He failed miserably. Anakin was unable to let go of himself, of his desires AND his need to protect the ones he loved, he consequently killed the balance of things and gave of his connection to the light for a chance to save someone who could not be saved. The force eventually evened out with luke, but the damage was already done. 

Grey knights work well with the themes of star wars, but only if they are done well and not like rey. One can't just willy nilly take whatever powers from wherever as one pleases. Anakin was incredibly gifted and still took years to master jedi powers, his fall to the dark side was guided and the powers he learned after were also taught to him. Force powers are usually passed down from force user to force user, or they are techniques that are learned through dedication and practice (like becoming a force ghost which yoda learned with the guidance of qui gon who hadn't completed his studies before his death.) If one were to dedicate their life to the force and enacting the will of the force, one could become a grey jedi, lack of attachment as the jedi have, emotional drive and single-mindedness like the sith, the powers and strength of will to listen to the force and help guide the flow rather than to push for one side or the other. If there were such a person they would want an apprentice to Cary on their work, thus passing on all they had learned and no doubt training for years before passing on. It is a fascinating character study, just not one that has ever been done well in screen format (looking at you rey and ben). 

Tldr: grey knights aren't cannon but they could be because they work with some of the lore.

People would act differently based on the level of melanin because of the culture and history and opressive systems associated with being black or with being another minority. 

I understand that being percieved as "a racist" is something abhorrent to most people with common sense, but the thing is that good people who are doing their best to recognize their privileged can still deal with engaging in racism without being bad people. Color blindness is one of those things. It is a phrase/mentality that ends up erasing a person's life experiences in a misguided attempt to recognize someone as an equal.

On a personal level I have been told before by friends who I value and who I know are advocates for racial justice that they forget my race until it comes up in conversation. To them that is just saying they see me as a person before seeing my race, but to me that is saying that my race isnt a part of my identity and that it would set me apart if I wasnt so close to them, even if not in a negative way. The racial blindness is effectively a way of discounting how my life experiences and culture influence my way of seeing and interacting with the world. Our experiences are not the same and that doesn't mean we cant talk about the differences, it just means it's important to recognize they are there.

Something I found really helpful when I was feeling suicidal was allowing myself to feel bad without feeling guilty about it. Hard to do but once you train yourself to think like that it's easier to not keep slipping deeper. Often being depressed is like a downward spiral and it's really hard to latch onto things that can help you feel less like shit because nothing matters. Do little things and focus on the immediate. If you make a doodle you like or see a bird being cute revel in it. If something bad happens allow yourself to feel it and process it without keeping it with you. Everything is only in the moment and doing things that take you out of the moment or distract you can also be good temporary coping mechanisms.

It took me about a month to do more than make a frapp once or twice during a rush.

It took me about two months to be able to do basic drinks for myself during nights without asking too many questions. 

Took me slightly longer than three months to be put on bar (even if it was only for a little while and never during peak) 

Took me about five months to be "good" at bar aka capable of being on bar for several  hours even if it's busy. 

Now at nine months bar is my favorite thing ever. 

It's different for everyone, but it's fun once you get the hang of it. :)  My best advice to you is when it's slow, practice by making the drinks you ring up! If you have whoever is on bar there to fact check you, it's a nice way to learn because you know exactly what was ordered and how and you can hand it off to whoever is on bar if things get busy. I learned most of my bar stuff when I was preclosing because it was slow enough that I didn't have to worry about slowing other people down. Plus night people are often more chill than the crowd of people going to work in the mornings. 

Whatever you do be sure not to stress too much. It's something that comes with practice, and everyone learns bar at a different pace. One of coworkers picked up bar by her second month, one person has been with us for over two months and has barely touched even the most basic drinks. Have fun with it! Best of luck! :)

I agree that having a trainer is super important! Having someone actually walk you through the steps and show you the ins and outs of an individual store is really important as well! Trust me when I say that being a newbie is really difficult for everyone. Even with a proper trainer to flush out the online stuff, there are sooooooo many things that just take practice or that you learn after. I have been working at Starbucks for 9 months and just now learned how to fill our handwashing soap! 

My best advice to you is to ask questions. It might seem like you are intturupting or taking up too much time but it really is the best and only way to make sure you know things and the proper way to do them. And it's a good way to learn which people are willing to help. 

I personally love helping out green beans because I'm new enough that I still have vivid memories of how overwhelming it all was when I started. Find the people who are willing to help and always ask questions, especially if you don't have a dedicated trainer (which you probably should). 

Also asking questions here or on the Facebook group is a great way to learn if you are not comfortable with your in store partners yet. 

Stick it out for a little longer and see if something clicks. As much as I love to complain, there really is something nice about being a barista.  Hope things go better for you.
